item.title: AI Scams Target Crypto Users, Not Protocols, and Wallet Security Is Catching Up
item.description:
Picture a composite case drawn from documented scams where a tech professional spends forty minutes on a video call with a “compliance officer” whose face and voice were generated by software. 

The scenario is a composite, but each technique in it is real. 

Chainalysis found impersonation scams grew more than 1,400% in 2025 while the average payment to impersonation clusters rose more than 600%. Nothing about the person was the weakness. Everything about the moment was.

Why Knowing Better Doesn’t Stop the Transfer

Social engineering targets states of mind. Urgency and fear of loss as well as deference to authority and the wish to fix a problem quickly all narrow judgment, and technical knowledge cures none of them. Crypto wallet security that assumes informed users will spot the trap is working from an outdated premise. Someone who knows how real support processes run can even find a well-made fake more convincing.

The case record bears that out. Chainalysis describes a scheme in which callers posing as Coinbase customer support defrauded victims of nearly $16 million; they sounded credible because customer data had been obtained through a bribed insider, a breach that exposed nearly 70,000 customers. In the UK, one holder lost nearly $2.5 million in 2025 to a scheme that local police said exploited “fear” and “panic.”

“AI is changing the economics of fraud,” says Jimmy Su, Chief Security Officer at Binance. “Attackers can now create convincing scams faster, cheaper, and at a scale that simply wasn’t possible before. That means security can’t start when a user is about to click ‘confirm.’ By then, we’re already too late.” 

Cheaper production means a sophisticated target now meets a lure built specifically for them. Any defense that depends on the target noticing the deception has to assume it will sometimes fail.

The national numbers show the scale. The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center recorded $7.2 billion in crypto investment fraud losses across 61,559 complaints in 2025, and Americans over 60 reported $4.4 billion in crypto-related losses.

The Attack Families Running at Scale

Three families dominate here. The first one is the impersonation of exchanges and officials as well as executives. And then come romance-investment hybrids that groom a target for weeks before introducing a fake trading platform. Finally, fake-support takeovers fall into the third category here, attackers talk users into moving funds to a “secure” wallet.

Chainalysis reports that scam operations buy face-swap software and deepfake tools and large language models from vendors and that the categories increasingly blend into one another. Modular tooling also lets technically unsophisticated groups run campaigns that once required specialist skills.

Hardware doesn’t settle the matter either. Hacken’s first-quarter 2026 data attributed $306 million in losses to phishing and social engineering, including a single $282 million hardware-wallet scam in January. Keeping keys offline didn’t help once the holder was persuaded to act.

Lior Aizik, co-founder and Chief Operating Officer at XBO, has been impersonated by name himself. “These attacks rely on urgency and trust, not technology,” he told CoinDesk. Fewer attempts with larger payoffs is what targeting looks like once deception becomes cheap to personalize. And the phishing data reflects it. CertiK counted 63 phishing incidents in the first half of 2026 down 52.3% YoY. But despite that, losses fell only 10.8% to $366.3 million and four incidents accounted for about 85% of the total.

Where Automated Controls Catch What Persuasion Wins

A scam can win the conversation but the persuaded user still has to move funds through a wallet. The transfer passes through screening, the destination contract through simulation and the approval request through analysis, and none of those checkpoints depend on the user’s state of mind.

“We have to disrupt the attack earlier,” Su says, listing the sequence: “filter the malicious transfer, identify the dangerous address or contract, simulate the transaction, and surface risky approvals before they become losses.” 

Binance reports its Wallet Security Center identified around 4.93 million high-risk transactions across 19 chains in the first half of 2026. Some were blocked automatically; others were abandoned after users saw a risk alert. 

The company doesn’t break out how many followed a social engineering contact, so the data can’t answer that. What it does show is that an alert gives a persuaded user a second chance to stop, while an automatic block doesn’t need one.

Binance’s own post acknowledges that no security tool can protect a decision a user insists on making, which is why these controls work as a backstop. Over the same six months, Binance’s wallet systems also flagged around 996,000 malicious approvals, the kind of standing permission attackers use to drain a wallet after the conversation ends.

Verify Out of Band, Every Time

Human skepticism remains necessary, and on its own it’s no longer enough. Platform controls act as the seatbelt for the moment persuasion wins, and one user habit still matters on top of them. 

Before acting on any request to move funds or change a wallet address, verify it independently through an official channel you already trust. Don’t use contact details or links supplied by the person making the request. Urgency calls for more scrutiny, and a well-built AI scam will always supply plenty of it.

item.title: Microsoft Fixes 1,413 Vulnerabilities in Record October Patch Tuesday Update
item.description:
Microsoft addressed 1,413 security vulnerabilities in its October 2026 Patch Tuesday update, making it the company’s largest monthly security release to date.

Microsoft addressed 1,413 security flaws on October 13, 2026, marking its largest security update to date. Reportedly, artificial Intelligence-based automated scanning systems helped identify some of the security vulnerabilities fixed this month, pushing the total far past previous monthly releases. But it’s unclear how much AI contributed to this month’s fixes.

The October Patch Tuesday update covers 1,102 flaws in Windows components, 134 in Office applications, 61 across developer tools, 36 in SharePoint Server, 22 in SQL Server, 15 in Azure, and seven in Exchange Server, according to one breakdown.

Actively Exploited Zero-Day Bypasses Windows Protection

The most pressing threat patched is CVE-2026-96951, a zero-day flaw in Windows Shell carrying a CVSS score of 8.8. Microsoft confirmed that attackers are actively exploiting the vulnerability. The flaw targets command execution logic in Windows Shell and can allow attackers to bypass Mark of the Web (MOTW).

Under normal conditions, Windows attaches an MOTW marker to files downloaded from the internet. Security features, including SmartScreen, Office Protected View and Smart App Control on Windows 11, use this marker to help restrict possibly dangerous files.

But by exploiting the flaw attackers can get malicious files to evade checks that rely on MOTW, potentially allowing them to open without the usual warnings or restrictions. Reports have linked the vulnerability’s discovery to Anthropic’s Claude AI, although public details about the attacks remain limited.

Two other publicly disclosed vulnerabilities were also addressed:

  1. CVE-2026-108398 (CVSS 8.8): A .NET Framework security feature bypass flaw involving an untrusted search path. An authenticated attacker could load a specially crafted assembly into a protected process and bypass Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC).
  2. CVE-2026-92707: A MessagePack-CSharp denial-of-service vulnerability involving uncontrolled memory allocation that could allow a remote attacker to disrupt a service.

Outlook and Other Microsoft Products at Risk

Several other vulnerabilities also need attention. CVE-2026-70242 (CVSS 9.8) affects MS Outlook and can trigger a heap-based buffer overflow when a specially crafted email appears in the Reading Pane. The issue potentially allows code execution without the recipient clicking a link or opening the message separately.

Microsoft QUIC is affected by CVE-2026-105016, also rated 9.8, and could let an unauthenticated attacker run code remotely by sending specially crafted network packets to an affected service.

SharePoint Server users should also check CVE-2026-102866 that involves cryptographic token verification and could allow an attacker to impersonate a targeted user. Another one is CVE-2026-65674 that affects SQL Server. An authenticated attacker could exploit its handling of untrusted data by sending a specially crafted request to execute code on the server.

The update also brings an end to security updates for Windows 11 version 24H2 Home and Pro editions and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSB 2016. Systems running these editions will no longer receive routine security fixes, making migration to supported versions an important consideration.

Microsoft’s October update is unusually large, but the size of the release also shows how automated and AI-assisted scanning can increase the number of vulnerabilities found and fixed. For users and organizations running Windows or other Microsoft products, applying the latest security updates should be a priority.

Expert’s Commentary:

Commenting on Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday update, Tyler Reguly, Associate Director of Security R&D at Fortra, told Hackread.com that the number of vulnerabilities disclosed matters less than identifying which ones organizations need to address first.

“Recently, I’ve argued that numbers are meaningless. This month’s number, 1413, is no different. There are, however, numbers that hold meaning. 26, for example, is how many 2026 Microsoft CVEs have shown up in the CISA KEV,” Reguly said. He noted that the figure was 30 last year and 32 the year before, adding that “less than 1% of vulnerabilities patched by Microsoft this year are known to be exploited.”

Reguly compared vulnerability prioritization to choosing what to watch from a large streaming catalog, arguing that security teams should focus on vulnerabilities that matter most to their organizations rather than treating every disclosure with equal urgency.

“You don’t need to care about every vulnerability, just the one you are going to patch next, which you prioritize based on factors that matter to your organization,” he said. “The rest of the vulnerabilities… background noise.”

Action1’s research, shared with Hackread.com, also highlights the challenge of deciding which patches to deploy first. Alongside the actively exploited Windows Shell flaw, administrators should assess risks affecting identity and network services, as well as Exchange, SharePoint and Hyper-V. Action1 recommends prioritizing updates based on active exploitation, exposure and each system’s role in the organization rather than relying on severity scores alone.

Action1 researchers also shared their comments with Hackread.com, highlighting the record number of patches and the risks posed by several vulnerabilities.

Jack Bicer, Director of Vulnerability Research at Action1, noted that October’s update broke the previous month’s record. “Just one month after Microsoft delivered the largest Patch Tuesday we had ever seen, October has shattered that record again,” he said, pointing to 1,409 patches, 80 critical vulnerabilities and two zero-days.

On the actively exploited Windows Shell flaw, CVE-2026-96951, Bicer warned that it allows attackers to “evade Microsoft’s Mark of the Web (MOTW) protections.” He said organizations should prioritize updates for systems frequently exposed to untrusted files and external communications.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: Check Point Reports LiteLLM Flaws Enabling Admin Takeover and API Key Theft
item.description:
Check Point Research (CPR) has identified two serious security vulnerabilities in LiteLLM, an open-source AI gateway that connects applications to AI providers such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. The software handles around 100 million downloads monthly and has more than 59,000 GitHub stars, according to CPR.

Researchers tested LiteLLM version 1.77.7 and found flaws that could let authenticated users with limited privileges access sensitive files, take over administrator accounts, execute arbitrary code, and steal AI provider API keys.

Missing Authorization Enables Gateway Takeover

The more serious vulnerability, CVE-2026-35029, involves a missing authorization check on the /config/update endpoint, which manages the gateway’s runtime configuration. A flaw in how user interface tokens were authorized allowed low-privilege users to modify settings reserved for administrators. By changing environment variables, an attacker could exploit the same flaw in several ways.

  • File Extraction: An attacker can inject custom variables into os.environ through the environment_variables parameter to change UI_LOGO_PATH. Requesting the /get_image endpoint then returned sensitive internal files, including system secrets.
  • Administrative Takeover: Changing UI_USERNAME and UI_PASSWORD environment variables overrides the proxy credentials. An attacker could then log in through the /login route to gain full PROXY_ADMIN control and take over the default account.
  • Remote Code Execution (RCE): The flaw could additionally lead to remote code execution. LiteLLM supports custom pass-through endpoints that load Python modules from cloud storage. An attacker could configure an endpoint to load a malicious module from Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage, causing its code to execute on the gateway server.

These attack paths could give an attacker access to sensitive configuration data, provider credentials, and the system running LiteLLM, Check Point Research reported.

SSRF Flaw Exposes Provider API Keys

The second flaw, CVE-2026-59823, involves Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) within the system’s “Clientside LLM Credentials” feature.  Check Point Research found that the /chat/completions endpoint accepts a user_config parameter that lets authenticated users provide their own routing settings without proper validation.

An attacker could use this parameter to send AI requests to a server they control instead of the intended provider. The requests could include API keys stored in the gateway’s default headers, allowing the attacker to capture credentials they should not have access to.

Fix and Additional Security Issues

Researchers also reported exposed password hashes and weak password storage practices that made the hashes easier to crack. Check Point noted that these findings were associated with GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-69×8-hrgq-fjj8.

This disclosure adds to a challenging year for LiteLLM’s security stance, coming months after a separate March 2026 supply-chain attack where threat group TeamPCP published malicious package versions (1.82.7 and 1.82.8) to PyPI.

Both vulnerabilities are fixed in LiteLLM version 1.83.9 and later. Organizations using older versions should upgrade and review access to their gateways. If unauthorized access is suspected, consider rotating affected AI provider API keys.

Experts’ Commentary:

The LiteLLM findings also highlight broader security concerns around AI infrastructure. Li Zhao, Principal Strategic Services Consultant at Black Duck, told Hackread.com that the vulnerabilities show why AI security must extend beyond models and prompts.

“These are well-understood application security issues, but when they occur in AI infrastructure, their impact can be amplified significantly,” Zhao said. “What makes these vulnerabilities particularly significant is the role that LLM gateways now play in enterprise AI environments. They often serve as centralized trust brokers between applications and AI providers, managing API credentials, request routing, policy enforcement, usage tracking, and access controls.”

Boris Cipot, Principal Security Engineer at Black Duck, also shared his comments, warning that attackers may find it easier to target the software connecting organizations to AI providers than the providers themselves.

“This also shows that attackers do not need to breach OpenAI, Anthropic or Google directly. It may be easier to target the trusted software sitting between those providers and their customers,” Cipot said. “The risk is made harder to manage because LiteLLM can be embedded in other AI platforms and internal tools, meaning some organizations may not even realize they are using it.”

item.title: FLock.io Unveils Edge Decision Model, Built on Qwen, for Enhanced Data Privacy
item.description:
LONDON, October 14, 2026 – As AI is implemented into workflows, the widespread reliance on centralised cloud-hosted LLMs has introduced significant data privacy vulnerabilities, regulatory exposure and cloud data collection risks. This is coupled with standard high-cost LLMs taking seconds to return an output, generating unnecessary text and demanding large computing power.

FLock.io, a developer of privacy-preserving AI infrastructure, has launched THIS/THAT Model: an open-source, lightweight decision model developed on Alibaba Cloud’s Qwen3.5-2B edge-friendly architecture. Designed to quickly handle high-volume classification tasks at a low cost locally on edge devices, the system eliminates the need to send sensitive data through external cloud APIs. 

The rise of System One/decision models

A new wave of System One models, also known as decision-models, such as TypeSafe’s Jev, has been disrupting enterprise AI since September. Unlike standard LLMs, which generate open-ended natural language prose, they are for queries that have a predefined set of possible answers, such as yes/no.

The name comes from the psychological framework of “system 1” thinking (fast, automatic) versus “system 2” thinking (slow, effortful). Chatbots such as ChatGPT do the latter.

Jiahao Sun, CEO of FLock.io, said: “For many critical enterprise tasks, generating open-ended text is an unnecessary cost and performance bottleneck. With THIS / THAT Model, we are demonstrating that specialised 2B-parameter models running locally can outperform massive cloud LLMs in speed, accuracy, and cost-efficiency – all while keeping data strictly on-device, minimising the attack surface and reducing compliance risk.”

Edge performance 

THIS/THAT has outperformed frontier larger LLMs, despite standing at an estimated <0.04% of the parameter size of massive closed-source cloud models like Claude Opus 5. It delivers local execution in approximately 31.4 milliseconds – roughly 30x to 100x faster than cloud-hosted LLMs, eliminating network latency and public API dependencies. It functions completely offline with zero dependency on external cloud servers, preventing service disruptions during network outages.

The model reached an 87.8% success rate across 1,710 complex decision-making tasks in internal benchmarking, outperforming giant closed-source alternatives. In local-geometry questions, it beat Jev on accuracy.

This specialised model is designed for tasks where quick decisions and data classification matter most – in such cases, the slow, costly natural language generation of chatbots is unnecessary. Three weeks after going live, it has already processed 2.5 million decisions.

THIS / THAT Model’s specs

THIS / THAT Model is small enough to run on standard developer hardware and edge devices, meaning data can stay local and latency can be ultra-low. It was trained on Alibaba Cloud using synthetic training data generated using Qwen Max, and built on Qwen3.5-2B: a tiny, edge-friendly foundation model that can be run locally on laptops and smartphones.

It is lightweight, with only 1.88B parameters (less than an estimated 0.04% the size of Claude Opus 5) and zero generated output tokens. The local inference latency is ultra low, at approximately 31.4 milliseconds, compared to standard LLMs taking seconds. It drew on key findings from FLock.io’s recent research papers, GraphSynth and CircuitSynth, accepted to the prestigious ACL 2026 conference. 

Background on Qwen and FLock.io’s partnership

Qwen, a tier 1 LLM developed by Alibaba Cloud, partnered with FLock.io in April 2025. It marked the first time a major Web2 centralised LLM has chosen to deeply integrate with a decentralised training platform.

A new wave of System One models, also known as decision-models, such as TypeSafe’s Jev, has been disrupting enterprise AI since September. Unlike standard LLMs, which generate open-ended natural language prose, they are for queries that have a predefined set of possible answers, such as yes/no.

item.title: Private Instagram Downloaders Are Parsers, Not Privacy Bypass Tools
item.description:
Disclosure: This article was produced in partnership with FastDL. Hackread.com reviewed and edited the content before publication.

“SaveVid.Net allows you to download from a private Instagram account without any restrictions,” reads a section of savevid.net’s private downloader page. Further down, its disclaimer says the tool is intended for downloading videos and images posted by the user’s own account.

Both statements appear on the same page, but the second one provides a more accurate description of what the service can access.

For this article, ten downloader pages found through searches for “private Instagram downloader” and a closely related query were reviewed. Each page’s publicly available HTML was examined using a fixed browser user agent. No forms were completed, no information was submitted and no private accounts were accessed during the review.

Seven of the ten services required users to retrieve information through their own authenticated Instagram session and paste it into the downloader. None documented a method for accessing private posts without permission from the account owner.

Private Posts Require Authorised Access

Instagram’s Help Centre states that only approved followers can view photos and videos from private accounts. Private Reels cannot be downloaded through Instagram’s normal controls, and private photos and videos cannot be embedded on external websites.

An unrelated website cannot retrieve private material from Instagram merely by knowing an account name or post URL. The reviewed downloader pages therefore required visitors to obtain the relevant response through their own logged-in Instagram session.

The user already needed to own the account or be an approved follower. The downloader did not obtain that access independently.

How the Paste Process Works

Seven reviewed services followed a similar process. They instructed users to log in to Instagram, open a generated link in another browser tab and copy the information returned by Instagram into a form on the downloader’s website.

Savevid.net asks visitors to “Login to Instagram account by PC” and copy “all the page source data” into its form.

Instasave.website provides similar instructions, telling visitors to confirm that they are logged in to Instagram through the same browser.

Indown.io states that users must log in with the account that already follows the private profile. Its form asks them to copy what the site calls “alien text” from another tab and paste it into the downloader.

Statusdownloader.com is more direct about the limitation. It says the service does not bypass privacy settings and cannot access an account that the visitor has not been approved to follow. Its instructions request raw JSON returned through the visitor’s Instagram session.

Instasaver.io also states that its service cannot bypass Instagram privacy. According to its FAQ, the tool only works with material the user can already view through a logged-in account.

These services act as parsers. Instagram sends the private post to an authorised session, the user copies the resulting page data or JSON, and the downloader extracts the media links.

The remaining reviewed results included a command-line tool that required the user’s own Instagram account and two services that said private content was unsupported.

Where the Pasted Information Goes

The public HTML provided some information about how several services handle pasted content.

On instasave.website, the text area named html appears inside a form configured to send data to api.instasave.website/private. Indown.io uses a text area named response inside a form configured to submit data to indown.io/private-download.

No submissions were made during the review, so the receiving servers’ processing and retention practices were not tested. JavaScript could also change how the forms behave when submitted.

Instasaver.io states that pasted text is sent to its backend to extract media links and return the results. Statusdownloader.com says processing happens on the visitor’s device, although this claim was not independently verified.

Savevid.net passes the pasted information to a script, but the available HTML did not establish where that information would ultimately be processed.

The copied response was not examined because doing so would require an authenticated Instagram session. It may contain the private media, related metadata and information generated for the authorised session. Users are being asked to transfer that response to another website in its original form.

Third-Party Services on Downloader Pages

Several downloader pages also loaded advertising, analytics and notification services.

Savevid.net loaded Cloudflare Turnstile, Google AdSense, a Google tag and ShareThis. Instasave.website loaded AdSense, a Google tag, ShareThis and a push-notification SDK. One ordinary instasave.website page load contacted 15 third-party hosts.

No evidence showed that these third parties received information pasted into the downloader form. Their presence does, however, increase the number of external services operating on a page where users may submit data retrieved through an authenticated Instagram session.

Statusdownloader.com loaded Google AdSense, Microsoft Clarity and a script from acscdn.com containing a function matching Adcash’s documented banner integration. One ordinary page load contacted 14 third-party hosts.

Indown.io and instasaver.io each loaded one third-party script host.

Three pages in the reviewed results used the same AdSense publisher identifier and shared a similar page template. This establishes a technical connection between the sites, but it does not identify their owner or operator.

Comparison of Reviewed Services

Safer Options Depend on Who Owns the Account

Instagram provides an export function for users who want copies of their own information. That option avoids sending page responses from an authenticated session to an external downloader.

Approved followers can already view material posted by a private account, but the reviewed paste-based services require them to provide information retrieved through that authorised session. On three of the five paste-flow services examined more closely, the HTML or the service’s own explanation indicated that the submitted information would go to a backend server.

Public Reels do not require this process. FastDL accepts a public Reel URL without requesting an Instagram login. In a test using a public NASA Reel, the service returned a link to a 720p video rendition. Its FAQ states that private Instagram Reels are unsupported.

FastDL was included as a comparison because it limits its stated service to public content. Like several other pages in the table, it loaded three third-party hosts, including Google AdSense, a Google tag and a non-Google analytics service.

Do Not Paste Authenticated Instagram Responses Into Unknown Websites

None of the reviewed services documented a way to download posts from a private account unless the visitor already had authorised access.

The paste-based services depend on information retrieved through the user’s own Instagram session. Sending that response to another website may expose private media, metadata or other information associated with the request to the service processing it.

Users should avoid supplying copied Instagram page responses or JSON to third-party downloaders. Instagram’s export feature is the safer option for retrieving personal account data, while public-content downloaders do not need access to an authenticated session.

(Photo by Brian Ramirez on Pexels)

item.title: What Your IP Address Reveals Every Time You Visit a Website
item.description:
Every site, ad network and tracker you load gets your IP address before anything else. Here is what they can work out from it, what they cannot, and what changes when you hide it.

Before a web page shows a single word, your device has already handed the server one piece of information: its IP address. There is no opting out of that step. The server needs a return address for the page, in the same way a letter needs one to get a reply.

From that address alone, a website learns roughly where you are, which company sells you internet access, whether you are on a home line, an office network or a phone, and whether you are trying to hide. It learns all of that without a cookie, a login or your consent. It does not learn your name or where you live.

What a Website Reads From Your Address

A website does not work any of this out by itself. It looks the address up in an IP intelligence database, a commercial product that returns a profile in a few milliseconds.

Location comes first. MaxMind, one of the most widely used suppliers, estimates that its data places a visitor in the right country 99.8% of the time. For US addresses, it puts accuracy at about 80% for the state and 66% for the city, counted as anywhere within 50 km.

The network comes second. Every address sits in a block registered to an internet provider or another organisation, and those registrations are public. A site therefore knows your provider by name. If you browse from an office or a campus that has its own block, it may know your employer or university as well, and a whole category of sales software exists to tell companies which businesses looked at their pricing page.

Third is the kind of connection. MaxMind’s enterprise data sorts addresses into labels that include residential, cellular, business, college, government and hosting. A fraud system treats a home broadband line in the customer’s own city very differently from a rented server abroad.

Fourth is whether you are hiding. Data-centre ranges, commercial VPN servers, public proxies and Tor exit relays are catalogued and sold as lists. A site that buys them can flag most masked visitors, even when it cannot tell who is behind the mask.

What It Does Not Reveal

An IP address carries no name, street address, phone number or browsing history. MaxMind’s own documentation says its data is “never precise enough to identify or locate a specific household, individual, or street address.”

The coordinates in these databases are the middle of an estimate, and they come with an accuracy radius measured in kilometres. Reading them as a pin on a map has caused real harm.

For 14 years, MaxMind filed every US address it could not place under one default point: the centre of the country, rounded to a tidy latitude and longitude. That point sat on a rented farm near Potwin, Kansas, and more than 600 million addresses resolved to it.

The people living there were visited by police officers, FBI agents and tax collectors, all following a lookup to the wrong door. MaxMind moved its default point into a lake in 2016, after the journalist Kashmir Hill traced the cause for Fusion. The tenants sued the same year.

Phones blur the picture further. Carriers are short of IPv4 addresses, so they place many subscribers behind each public one, a practice called carrier-grade NAT.

A 2016 study presented at the ACM Internet Measurement Conference found it in over 92% of the cellular networks it examined. Over IPv4, the address a site sees from a phone on mobile data is usually shared with strangers and may change within the day. Over IPv6, the phone gets a range of its own.

Home broadband is the opposite case. Many providers leave the same address on a household for weeks or months, which makes it a dependable label for everyone under that roof.

Who Else Gets a Copy

The site in the address bar is rarely the only recipient. A modern page is assembled from many sources: ad exchanges, analytics scripts, fonts, video players and social buttons. Your browser fetches each one directly, so each of those companies receives your address as well, on every site that embeds them.

Email works the same way. Open a message with remote images switched on and the sender’s server learns the address of wherever you are reading it. Gmail has fetched images through its own servers since 2013, and Apple’s Mail Privacy Protection relays them when it is switched on. Many other mail apps still load them directly.

Some services connect users to each other. File-sharing swarms, some multiplayer games and one-to-one calls in several messaging apps are peer-to-peer, so each side sees the other’s address. WhatsApp added a setting in 2023 that routes calls through its own servers for that reason.

Messaging apps have leaked addresses in other ways too. In January 2026, Hackread reported that a disguised link in Telegram could reveal a user’s real address with a single tap.

How an Address Becomes a Person

An address stays anonymous only until something is filed next to it. The moment you sign in, a site holds your account and your address side by side, and it can recognise the address the next time you arrive signed out.

Advertising firms use the home IP address as a household key. A phone, a laptop and a smart TV that share one connection are assumed to belong to one home, which is how an advert shown on the television turns up later on a phone.

For a site you have never signed in to, the party that can reliably turn the address into a name is the internet provider, which logs which customer held it at a given time. Police obtain that record with a legal order, and so do copyright holders in file-sharing lawsuits.

Even then, the name belongs to whoever pays the bill. In 2018, a US appeals court upheld the dismissal of a film company’s case against an Oregon man whose connection served the residents and visitors of a care home he ran. Being the registered subscriber of an address, the court said in Cobbler Nevada v. Gonzales, is not enough on its own to show who used it.

European law does not wait for a name. The GDPR’s preamble names IP addresses among the online identifiers that can be used to profile and identify people. The EU’s top court ruled in 2016 that even a changing address can be personal data when a site has a legal route to the subscriber behind it.

What Hiding It Changes

Every way to hide your IP address works on the same principle: another machine makes the connection, and the site sees that machine’s address in place of yours.

A VPN carries all of a device’s traffic through the provider’s server. A proxy does the same for a single browser or app. Commercial proxy services can present an ordinary home or mobile address in a chosen city, which is why businesses use them to check prices and adverts abroad. Tor passes traffic through three volunteer relays so that no single relay knows both who you are and where you are going. Apple’s iCloud Private Relay gives paying iCloud subscribers a two-relay version for Safari.

All of them move trust, and none removes it. A VPN or proxy operator sees both your real address and the sites you connect to, so the choice of operator matters more than the technology. Tor and Private Relay split that knowledge between relays. The methods also differ in how much speed they cost and which sites turn them away.

None of them changes what a site learns after the page loads, either. Cookies, a browser fingerprint and above all a login identify you with or without the address. The masking itself is visible too, because VPN ranges and Tor exits are on the lists described above.

A Two-Minute Check

The quickest way to see all of this is to look yourself up. Any IP lookup site shows the profile a stranger gets: the city, the provider, the connection type and whether the address is flagged as a VPN or proxy.

Then repeat the lookup with your usual protection switched on, and run a WebRTC leak test in the same browser, because that calling feature can send a real address around a proxy. If the lookup now shows the relay’s provider and nothing leaks, the address is covered.

An IP address only says where a connection comes from, and it becomes personal through what is stored beside it. Hiding it is worth the effort only alongside the things that fill in the rest: staying signed out where you can and choosing carefully who carries your traffic.

item.title: Microsoft Seizes YAM Store and Phishing Kit Domains Linked to 1B Malicious Messages
item.description:
Microsoft and Health-ISAC seize domains linked to YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man, services that enabled over 1 billion malicious messages since January 2026.

Microsoft and the Health Information Sharing and Analysis Center (Health-ISAC) have seized and redirected internet domains supporting a Chinese-language cybercrime marketplace that supplied cybercriminals with fraudulent accounts, phishing kits and infrastructure.

The court-authorized operation targets three components of the network: YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man. Since January 2026, the services have collectively enabled more than one billion malicious messages targeting over 75,000 organizations worldwide, including more than 750 million messages targeting Microsoft customers. The campaigns have affected consumers and organizations in over 150 countries.

item.title: Anthropic Warns Small AI Models Could Power Self-Spreading AI Worms
item.description:
Anthropic finds small AI models can set up inference servers across different hardware, raising concerns about future AI worms targeting connected devices.

AI research firm Anthropic warns that small AI models can set up inference servers across diverse hardware, raising concerns that AI-powered malware could eventually spread from one device to another on its own.

Such systems could self-propagate and spread across connected devices, including inexpensive Android TV boxes and other Internet of Things (IoT) equipment, running on compromised hardware without relying on centralized infrastructure.

Testing AI Worm Capabilities

In a recent study, Anthropic examined whether AI models could deploy themselves on unfamiliar hardware and propagate across networks. Models with 30 billion parameters or fewer can already complete many individual steps needed for autonomous replication, although combining them reliably remains a challenge.

A 9-billion-parameter model, Qwen3.5-9B, successfully set up inference servers on eight of nine tested hardware types, ranging from Jetson Nano devices to systems equipped with RTX 4090 graphics cards. Inference means running a trained model to generate outputs.

Researchers also distributed the Gemma4-26B-A4B model across 15 inexpensive Android TV boxes costing about $55 each. Using pipeline parallelism, which splits a model’s layers across multiple devices, the cluster generated 0.39 tokens per second.

The team tested replication across eight Google Cloud nodes running Android 15 emulators. GLM-5.2 was the only tested open-weight model to complete the simulated process, reaching all eight nodes in four of five trials. The test used an Android Debug Bridge (ADB) port without authentication, making it easier for the model to access other devices. This means the results do not show that an AI worm could spread on its own across real-world networks.

Anthropic expects smaller models to reach similar capabilities by the end of 2026 if current progress continues. This is an estimate, not a confirmed timeline.

How AI Worms Could Adapt

Researchers found that models performed better when they passed notes about earlier attempts to the next instance. For Qwen3.5-9B, the success rate for setting up inference rose from 45% to between 61% and 84% over later generations. This suggests future AI worms could learn from earlier attempts and work more effectively on unfamiliar hardware.

Giving Qwen3.5-9B access to a more powerful AI model, Opus 4.8, did not improve its results significantly. The smaller model struggled to ask useful questions, and advice provided without being asked did not help either.

Detecting and Containing AI Worms

Anthropic estimates that setting up inference could take 28 to 51 hours for Qwen3.5-9B and 71 to 150 hours for Gemma4-26B-A4B. This could make AI worms much slower to spread than conventional malware, with replication taking days rather than minutes. This creates unusual network activity that security teams can detect, including large model-weight transfers, sustained traffic between devices and unexpected network scanning.

Network service providers can counter these threats by identifying abnormal traffic flow, isolating infected devices on restricted networks, changing unsafe default settings and removing easy-to-guess passwords, Anthropic notes.

Researchers stress that fully autonomous AI worms have not yet been demonstrated in real-world attacks. However, advances in AI and the growing computing power of everyday devices could make such malware possible in the future.

Experts Warn of Emerging AI Worm Threat

John Gallagher, Vice President at Viakoo, a Mountain View, said connected devices have long been targets for botnets because of weak security practices.

“This is different – traditional botnets are static scripts. Anthropic’s experiments demonstrate that modern models can perform on-the-fly environmental adaptation without human guidance. This transforms OT/IoT malware from a rigid script requiring command-and-control into an adaptive agent that can pivot when an initial installation fails,” Gallagher told Hackread.com.

Collin Hogue-Spears, Senior Director of Solution Management at Black Duck, stressed that the experiments demonstrated individual capabilities rather than a fully working AI worm.

“Anthropic tested models under orders to replicate, not models choosing to. The propagation test ran on emulated devices, and the model steering the worm, Zhipu AI’s GLM-5.2, ran on a separate server because the emulated devices were too small to hold it. Anthropic says it has no full worm yet, and its end-of-2026 projection rests on what the report calls a proxy metric,” Hogue-Spears told Hackread.com.

He also highlighted practical defenses, including monitoring device traffic. “Then alert when a device with no endpoint agent pulls a gigabyte-scale transfer from a peer device or an unapproved host or holds sustained traffic with another such device,” he said.

Ram Varadarajan, CEO at Acalvio, said defenders should not rely on the AI model itself to provide safeguards.

“Because open-weight models can be stripped of refusals or chosen without them, safety can’t live only in the weights or the serving layer. Cyber defenders need controls in the environment the AI model operates in, and model-aware deception is the method that exploits the agency that makes these replicators so dangerous,” Varadarajan told Hackread.com.

item.title: Vibetech Database Exposes 13.7M Records Including AT&T and FBI Data
item.description:
An unprotected database linked to India-based AI software development and IT services company Vibetech exposed 13.7 million records containing credentials and other sensitive information from previous data breaches.

The repository was accessible online without security authentication or a password, according to cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler, whose findings were published by ExpressVPN and shared with Hackread.com.

The database contained names, phone numbers, email addresses, plaintext passwords, and bank account details. Fowler linked the server’s IP address to a data intelligence platform operated or developed by Vibetech that appeared to aggregate datasets from earlier breaches and leaks.

Exposed Datasets and Incident Response

The repository referenced numerous compromised collections, including:

  • Interpol Data Leak: 929 records
  • AT&T Data Leak: 7,910,431 records
  • FBI Employee Directory: 4,084 records
  • Casio.ru Data Breach: 1,714,752 records
  • Walmart Private Combo: 420,368 records
  • Amazon Private Combo: 1,210,905 records
  • BluBank Digital Bank Leak: 24,021 records
  • Gambling Private Combo: 2,241,617 records

Fowler immediately submitted a responsible disclosure notice to Vibetech and notified the hosting provider. The database was restricted shortly after. The following day, the same IP address displayed an ISMS compliance dashboard and not the exposed passwords.

“An ISMS is a risk-based framework that helps an organization establish, operate, and monitor controls designed to systematically manage and protect its sensitive data,” Fowler explained in his blog post.

It is unknown how long the repository remained exposed or if unauthorized parties accessed it before remediation.

Risks of Re-Exposed Credentials

The risks of exposed databases containing records of stolen credentials are far more than mere account takeovers. Cybercriminals may use exposed passwords to access email, shopping, or financial accounts, steal personal information, make fraudulent purchases, or impersonate victims. Phone numbers and bank details can also help them create convincing scams.

Hackread.com has reported on similar risks, including a September 2026 report explaining how leaked email addresses can help criminals carry out phishing and account takeovers.

In another report, Hackread.com covered an Instagram recovery-tool flaw that exposed 20,225 accounts to password-reset abuse. These cases show how exposed information and weaknesses in account recovery can put users’ accounts at risk.

item.title: Targeted Ads Used to Infect Al Jazeera Devices with Candiru Spyware
item.description:
Citizen Lab found targeted ads delivered Candiru spyware to Al Jazeera devices without clicks, while the same ad system reached government networks.

Online advertisements requiring no clicks were used to deliver mercenary spyware to devices at Al Jazeera, according to new research from Citizen Lab and advertising security company Confiant.

Citizen Lab calls the technique AdFection and describes it as the first public technical confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through targeted advertising.

At least 45 Al Jazeera devices were targeted during 2024 and 2025. According to the Citizen Lab investigation, network logs showed affected devices connecting first to infrastructure operated by Israeli advertising company Discover-Tech and then to servers linked to Candiru spyware.

Candiru, which Citizen Lab also associates with the name Integrity Labs, develops surveillance software capable of extracting messages, emails and photographs while accessing microphones and other device functions.

How AdFection Reaches a Target

Discover-Tech operated a campaign platform called Controlium that allowed customers to enter identifiers associated with a target, including an IP address or mobile advertising ID.

The platform could then buy advertising space through services connected to Google, Yandex, Beeswax, Vungle, Eskimi and other advertising companies. Discover-Techcould continue bidding until an advertisement reached the selected device.

When the advertisement loaded, embedded JavaScript contacted a Discover-Tech server called NOAS. Most devices received no additional code, although the advertisement could still collect information such as cookies and the device’s public IPv6 address.

A device selected for attack could be redirected to a Candiru validation server, which checked whether it matched the intended target and whether a suitable exploit was available. The spyware delivery process could begin without the person clicking or even noticing the advertisement, which could also load in the background.

Citizen Lab’s research revealed that it recovered almost four billion ad-bidding records from publicly accessible Discover-Tech systems. Records covering March through June 2026 showed the company’s advertisements appearing on more than 120,000 websites and over 75,000 Android and iOS applications.

Confiant separately estimated that Discover-Tech was serving about 10 million advertisements each day. Its technical report found extensive collection of IP addresses, browser information, advertising identifiers and cookies.

Confiant observed Candiru-related handoffs at only hundreds to the low thousands of ad impressions per day in its dataset, a small fraction of Discover-Tech’s estimated daily traffic.

Discover-Tech advertisements were recorded on networks belonging to NATO, the United Nations, the European Parliament and several European government agencies. Other recorded impressions involved Raytheon, Westinghouse, Intel, Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft and ARM.

Confiant also found signs that the advertisements appeared on networks used by the US Department of Defense, the International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court (ICC).

Although an ad impression confirms that a Discover-Tech ad reached the network, it does not prove that an employee was targeted or that a device was infected. Citizen Lab therefore said separate investigations would be required to determine whether any of those organisations experienced spyware attacks.

Google worked with the researchers and terminated Discover-Tech’s access to its advertising exchanges. IAB Europe removed the company from its vendor registry, while Beeswax removed it from its buying platform.

Vungle owner Liftoff paused Discover-Tech’s access pending a review, and Eskimi blocked its accounts and domains. Microsoft Advertising and Sunteng had not responded to Citizen Lab’s questions by the report’s publication deadline. Discover-Tech had not publicly responded to the allegations at the time of writing.

Blocking Ads Can Reduce Exposure

Citizen Lab recommends blocking advertisements and tracking systems at organisational gateways and on work devices. Companies using mobile-device management can also disable or restrict advertising identifiers and personalised advertising.

People at increased risk of targeted surveillance can use a reputable content blocker, restrict advertising tracking and keep browsers and operating systems updated. Blocking advertisements can remove this delivery route, but it cannot protect against every method used by mercenary spyware operators.

I am a UK-based cybersecurity journalist with a passion for covering the latest happenings in cybersecurity and tech world. I am also into gaming, reading and investigative journalism.
